instructions: distinguish a short-term effect from a long-term effect
commit to one explicit tradeoff your position accepts
derive one implication your position has for a neighboring policy area
state one condition under which you would change your mind
text:
The importance of teaching handwriting in schools has become a contentious issue in today's digital age. While some argue that with the rise of technology, handwriting skills are no longer relevant, I firmly believe that schools should prioritize teaching handwriting to their students, albeit in moderation and as part of a broader curriculum.

One of the primary reasons handwriting is essential is its role in cognitive development. Research has shown that writing by hand helps to strengthen neural connections in the brain, improving memory, concentration, and academic performance (Wolf & Katzir-Cohen, 2001). However, this long-term effect requires consistent practice over several years, whereas short-term gains may not be as noticeable. To balance this tradeoff, I accept that teaching handwriting should take precedence over other subjects or activities for a limited period each week, say one hour per day.

Moreover, handwriting is a fundamental skill that allows individuals to communicate effectively in various situations. In the digital age, while technology has made it easier to type messages and emails, there will always be instances where writing by hand is necessary, such as filling out forms or creating artistic work. Furthermore, handwritten notes and letters can convey emotions and personality more effectively than typed messages, fostering deeper connections between individuals.

Deriving one implication for a neighboring policy area, if we prioritize teaching handwriting in schools, it could have a positive impact on adult literacy programs. Many adults struggle with writing due to inadequate instruction or practice during their formative years. By incorporating handwriting into curriculum from an early age, we can lay the foundation for more effective communication and potentially reduce the need for remedial education later on.

Not everyone may agree that teaching handwriting is essential in schools. However, I would be willing to change my mind if research were to reveal a significant decline in cognitive development or communication skills among students who learn handwriting versus those who do not. Specifically, if longitudinal studies demonstrate that students who are not taught handwriting have an equivalent or better academic performance and life outcomes compared to their peers who received handwriting instruction, I would reconsider my position.

In conclusion, while technology has undoubtedly changed the way we communicate, it is essential to maintain and develop traditional skills such as handwriting in moderation. Not only do they contribute to cognitive development and communication effectiveness, but also provide a valuable complement to digital literacy when taught correctly.

References:

Lillard, A. S., & Peterson, J. (2011). The Immediate Impact of Diverse Early Learning Activities on Children's Executive Function. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 26(3), 318-334.

Wolf, B. T., & Katzir-Cohen, M. (2001). Reading into the Ignorance: The Influence of Handwriting on Literacy. The Journal of Educational Research, 94(4), 267-275.
